title: Broncos right guard Quinn Meinerz, on the impact of Davis Webb becoming the primary play-caller: "It's not a complete overhaul of the offense, but there's a lot of new, fun elements, new wrinkles, new stuff to it. Because when you get used to a system for so long, there's some of that beginner learning that you kind of like, miss out on. So, it's kind of nice to have a little refresh of things for us to have to learn on this offense for us to re-lock into and kind of -- it's not necessarily, like, monotonous. We have the same, the same, the same, the same. So, it's nice to have -- like, there's still some similar elements to this offense, but then there's a nice little like sprinkle of additions of what Davis has come up with, what Coach (Zach) Strief has come up with, what Chris Morgan has come up with. So, it's going to be good."

title: A couple of fans have asked me why Marlins are listening on Liam Hicks when he's cheap and highly productive. The thinking there: If another team sees him as a starting catcher (which he won't be here, of course, because of Mack), and is willing to pay the value that skilled hitting catchers generate in the trade market, they're compelled to listen. So they're not actively trying to trade him, but they will certainly listen. (Fairbanks, other relievers, Garrett are also available.)

I was not on my phone but I dropped my phone and it was stuck in my seat. I took my eyes off the road looking for my phone and my car veered into someone. It’s one of those roads where there’s no forgiveness. It’s one of those roads where I’ll teach my kids, you don’t drive in the left lane for no reason. You’re only allowed a foot. title: One point made in here: The $152M is the new money in the deal. Because the Eagles acted early with two years remaining on the deal, it folds into what they already owed and effectively becomes a six-year deal for around $183M. It's similar to how the Eagles did the DeVonta Smith deal two years ago (and likely the Quinyon Mitchell deal next offseason). If the team is aggressive, the player never hits the fifth-year option — it's a tool in putting together a new deal.

title: Mental Health check in from Seattle over by my @Seahawks training camp stop… PRACTICE BEING PROUD!!! My self talk is all often wayyyyy too negative. The roommates in my head are constantly telling me the worst things about myself. But instead of just letting them run rampant I started doing something to fight back against them. Every morning I now turn on a song and for the duration meditate by telling myself things I’m PROUD of about me. Over and over and over. That’s hard for a lot of us. Hard to the point I had to actually write a list on my phone so I can go back to them when my brain wants to go negative and start beating up on me again. The battle is on-going but I’ve had way more mornings now where I start the day kicking the gray’s ass instead of the other way around. Hope this helps. Let’s keep walking this walk together. Love y’all #mentalhealth #anxiety #depression #unbreakable

title: Bucs have reworked Mayfield's existing contract multiple times with void years to create short-term cap help, so there's $30.15 million in dead money that will count against the Bucs' salary cap after this deal is done. That's unavoidable. If the Bucs re-sign Mayfield before mid-February next year, they can keep the dead money split over three seasons -- basically $12 million each in 2027 and 2028 and $6 million in 2029. If they don't, all $30 million accelerates against the 2027 cap. The Bucs know this, and operate conceding some level of dead money as an interest-free loan against the constantly rising salary cap. So if Mayfield adds $18 million in extra dead cap, they're just going to restructure another major contract to a bonus to create cap space to offset that. What complicates that is using the franchise tag, which is inflexible and requires his full salary ($50 million or so) to count against the 2027 cap. Not ideal from a cap management standpoint.
